sections.title: Introduction

summary.text: Completes the glossary reference list (items 2–24) and introduces Chapter 1, framing the progression from paper-based records through digitization and digitalization to digital transformation (Fig. 1), situating person-centred point of service systems (PCPOSSs) within the 2019 WHO digital health guideline Recommendation 8 on digital client tracking with decision support (Fig. 2) and within an integrated primary health care digital ecosystem (Fig. 3), and explaining how workflow-based needs assessments and SMART Guidelines support PCPOSS implementation.

sections.title: Person-centred point of service systems

summary.text: Defines person-centred point of service systems (PCPOSSs) as digital systems combining decision support systems, community-based information systems, electronic health records, and personal health records across WHO digital health intervention classifications; contrasts the clerical and quality burdens of paper or siloed reporting systems with a combined PCPOSS built on the 'collect once, use for many purposes' principle (Fig. 4) and semantic/syntactic interoperability standards (such as ICD-11, SNOMED-GPS, and HL7 FHIR).

sections.extract: A person-centered point of service system (PCPOSS), digital in nature, facilitates the provision and delivery of health services to individuals (i.e. persons, clients, patients, health service users) at the point of care. A PCPOSS includes software capabilities that enable health- care providers to access, record and update individuals’ health information as well as interactively communicate with them. The term

sections.title: SMART Guidelines

summary.text: Summarizes the WHO SMART Guidelines approach and its five reusable knowledge layers—L1 Narrative (enhanced guidelines), L2 Operational (Digital adaptation kits), L3 Machine readable (implementation guides), L4 Executable (reference applications), and L5 Dynamic (precision health models)—and illustrates how countries adapt and localize these layers when implementing a PCPOSS (Fig. 5).

sections.extract: SMART Guidelines are Standards-based, Machine-readable, Adaptive, Requirements-based, and Testable recommended digital capabilities, health and data content. SMART Guidelines are WHO’s approach designed to systematize and accelerate the consistent application of recommended, life- saving interventions in the digital age (18). As countries are investing heavily in PCPOSSs, SMART Guidelines provide detailed

sections.title: How this handbook was developed

summary.text: Describes the handbook's development through expert consultations, implementation studies in Bangladesh, Pakistan, and Indonesia, the Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM), and the Principles for Digital Development ('establish people-first data practices' and 'design with people'), notes conflict-of-interest declarations, and introduces Chapter 2 on how stakeholders can use the software- and health-area-agnostic handbook.

sections.extract: This practical guide was developed from the experiences and feedback of a variety of experts and digital health practitioners. Experiences, insights, templates and feedback were gathered through a series of consultations, a working group, expert interviews and dedicated feedback sessions. This included lessons learned from a study on digitalizing paper-based routine health information systems across different

sections.title: Targeted scenarios of digital readiness

summary.text: Defines the two primary digital readiness scenarios targeted by the handbook: transitioning from a paper-only point-of-care system to an optimized digital system, and consolidating or upgrading partially digitized, siloed PCPOSSs operating alongside paper records into an integrated, interoperable PCPOSS.

sections.extract: This handbook was written with the intent to help articulate software and system requirements for a PCPOSS in these two key scenarios of digital readiness: Starting from a paper-only system: There are no PCPOSSs in place. Only paper-based records are being used at the point of care for the purposes of service delivery and reporting. The public health authority wants to optimize paper forms and transition to a

sections.title: Targeted users

summary.text: Identifies the primary audience of the handbook as business analysts, solution designers, health informaticians, public health programme teams, implementing partners, and software vendors bridging clinical/public health domains and technology, while emphasizing that end-users (health workers and health service users) must be actively engaged throughout requirements gathering, validation, and testing.

sections.extract: This handbook is aimed at individuals and teams seeking to gather and optimize the content and functional requirements for either adapting a PCPOSS or developing one bespoke. It is written for those with a public health and/or clinical background who have a baseline understanding of health information systems but may not be technologists themselves. In essence, this handbook is written for those who will fill the

sections.title: Before using this resource

summary.text: Outlines strategic and infrastructural prerequisites required before using the handbook—situating it in Phase 5 (Determining health content requirements) of the seven-phase digital health enterprise lifecycle (Fig. 6)—and provides a readiness checklist covering value proposition, alignment with national strategy, scope control, unique identification (Box 1), data privacy governance, sustainable financing, target end-users, product ownership, and interoperability.

sections.extract: The key assumption for users of this resource is that a comprehensive high-level needs assessment and strategic planning has already been conducted and concluded that implementing a PCPOSS is crucial for operationalizing a country’s digital health strategy. This needs assessment should have included a root-cause analysis illustrating the need for the PCPOSS to improve service delivery and accountability measures. If

sections.title: The stepwise approaches to digitizing

summary.text: Summarizes the four core phases structuring the handbook—understanding user requirements, undertaking design and adaptation, conducting training, testing and roll-out, and preparing for scale-up—and explains how teams apply them iteratively using agile prototyping and continuous user feedback loops from minimum viable product (MVP) to subsequent releases (Fig. 7).

sections.extract: Adhering to the Principles for Digital Development (see Annex 1), this handbook is organized in a stepwise manner that begins with the assumption of a limited or no digital system in place. It is a starting point for detailing plans to implement an enterprise-grade system planned for national scale up and integration with other national-level systems for long-term sustainability. sections.title: Choices for software and digital applications

summary.text: Clarifies that the handbook is software-neutral and recommends thorough documentation and collaboration tools during requirements gathering and design, then introduces Chapter 3 (Understand user requirements) with an overview of stakeholder roles, required strategic and clinical inputs, Annex worksheet tools (Annexes 3–13 and WHO DAKs), and expected requirements documentation outputs.

sections.extract: Implementation teams using this handbook are not expected to use any specific software applications during the requirements-gathering and detailed design processes. Regardless of the chosen technology used, the only strong recommendation would be to ensure robust, high-quality documentation of the requirements of the system and its design. Collaboration tools such as project management and file sharing tools (e.g.

sections.title: Follow key requirement-gathering methods

summary.text: Details four complementary requirement-gathering methods—desk reviews of local registers, reporting tools, and WHO Digital adaptation kits (DAKs); workplace observations of health workers with attention to minimizing the Hawthorne effect; semi-structured and follow-up interviews using broad-to-narrow questioning and the '5 Whys' root-cause technique (Fig. 8); and multi-stakeholder requirements-gathering validation workshops.

sections.extract: A combination of methods can be used to corroborate information and better guide the process outlined in this chapter for assessing needs and gathering requirements. Before outlining that process in the next sections of this chapter, this section provides an overview of some of these methods: desk review, semi-structured interviews, observations, follow-up interviews to verify observations, and

sections.title: Get to know the users

summary.text: Explains how to apply human-centred design to understand target users by creating comprehensive user personas (or interim proto-personas validated in the field) covering demographics, work environment, official and actual duties, challenges, and motivations; documenting illustrative use cases; and authoring structured 'As a… I want to… so that…' user stories that translate into functional requirements.

sections.extract: Following the first principle of digital development (design with the user), user-centred design starts with getting to know the people you are designing for through conversation, observation and co-creation. User personas, use cases and user stories are critical tools used in the design process to better understand exactly who the users are and what their needs are. Having an in-depth understanding of who the user

sections.title: Map business processes and workflows

summary.text: Describes how to inventory clinical and operational care pathways in a business process matrix (illustrated with the family planning DAK, Fig. 9), map current ('as-is') and optimized ('to-be') workflows using Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN 2.0) symbols (Table 1), label and annotate workflow steps (illustrated with the ANC DAK registration workflow, Figs. 10–11), and conduct as-is/to-be analyses to eliminate redundancies and bottlenecks.

sections.extract: Business processes are sets of related activities and tasks performed to achieve a specific objective (6–9). In health care, business processes include, among many other things, health service user registration, counselling, service provision and referral. Workflows are a visual representation of the progression of activities (tasks, events, interactions) performed within a business process (45). The specific

sections.title: Streamline data collection and indicator reporting

summary.text: Presents a five-step process for streamlining paper registers into a PCPOSS: inventorying primary service delivery and summary reporting forms (Annex 7), mapping form data elements in a consolidated spreadsheet (Annex 8), compiling aggregate indicators calculated from primary point-of-care data under the 'collect once, use for many purposes' principle (Annex 9), and removing duplicated, orphaned, or non-essential data elements.

sections.extract: Streamlining data collection is a long and tedious task, but it is the crux of translating paper register systems into a PCPOSS. The following are the five key steps needed to complete the streamlining. 1. Create an inventory of paper forms. 2. Map data elements across all forms. 3. Compile all aggregate indicators that need to be linked and reported. 4. Remove duplicated, orphaned and unnecessary data. 5.

sections.title: Create a data dictionary

summary.text: Provides the decision table for reconciling duplicated, non-essential, and orphaned data elements (Fig. 12 continuation) and explains how to construct a streamlined data dictionary—distinguishing database-design vs. UI-design data dictionaries—and map data elements to standardized semantic classifications and terminologies (such as WHO-FIC/ICD-11, LOINC, and SNOMED-GPS) and syntactic standards (HL7 FHIR), leveraging WHO DAKs and terminology services such as Open Concept Lab.

sections.extract: The final step in streamlining data collection and indicator reporting is to create a data dictionary, which (in this context) is a repository of all the data elements essential for individual and aggregate levels, including some metadata components, that will be included in the PCPOSS. For the purposes of designing the solution and facilitating understanding across multiple stakeholders, the data dictionary will

sections.title: Determine decision-support logic

summary.text: Explains how to document clinical care pathway decision-support logic—covering scheduling, clinical prompts, risk assessment/triage, and medical eligibility grounded in WHO or national guidelines—using a decision-support logic matrix (illustrated from the HIV DAK, Fig. 13), visual decision trees (illustrated from the ANC DAK, Fig. 14), and DMN-aligned decision-support tables (Annex 11).

sections.extract: Digital systems can go beyond simple data collection and aggregation by introducing additional layers of sophistication that are generally unavailable on paper. This includes the opportunity to enhance care provision with built-in decision-support logic. In PCPOSSs, embedded decision-support logic can help health workers follow appropriate clinical care pathways set out by WHO and national public health authorities’

sections.title: Map health service schedules

summary.text: Describes how to document recurring and prescribed health service schedules (such as antenatal care contacts, immunizations, and laboratory follow-ups) in spreadsheets organized by health worker occupational group, capturing trigger events, intervals, follow-up actions, expiration criteria, and schedule deviations (Annex 12).

sections.extract: Service schedules give health workers an overview of upcoming, due or overdue services, and aim to ensure timeliness of service delivery and continuity of care. Service schedules can also be a basis for reminders that are sent from the PCPOSS to health service users about upcoming services, if targeted health service user communication is an intervention included in the PCPOSS. Workflow mapping already completed by

sections.title: Gather and prioritize requirements

summary.text: Explains how to translate user stories, workflows, and data dictionaries into functional and non-functional requirements, prioritize them into high, medium, and low tiers using IEEE software requirements specification criteria (Annex 13), verify completion of Chapter 3 checkpoints, and transition to Chapter 4 (Undertake design and adaptation) with an overview of technology partner roles, inputs, tools, and outputs.

sections.extract: The requirements for a PCPOSS are the functional and non-functional criteria that it must meet to ensure end-users are satisfied and the system performs as intended. The following two types of requirements need to be gathered and prioritized. • Functional requirements describe what the system must be able to do (“the water bottle shall be able to store liquid without leaking” would be an everyday example). •

sections.title: Finalize software and vendor selection

summary.text: Outlines how to conduct an objective landscape analysis and scorecard evaluation to select software and vendors—including leveraging SMART Guidelines L4 executable reference applications such as the WHO Digital ANC module—and provides a four-part checklist covering pre-evaluation, software features and interoperability, software ownership and total cost of ownership, and vendor reputation and support.

sections.extract: After the requirements are defined and prioritized, the implementation team must first select and finalize a software and software vendor that can successfully achieve all necessary business requirements. The implementation team must conduct an objective software selection process comprising a landscape analysis to review tools that are already available in the market. A scorecard can be developed to compare

sections.title: Validate functional requirements

summary.text: Recommends holding iterative, component-by-component stakeholder workshops with the selected technology partner to validate and confirm functional requirements prior to software construction, ensuring alignment with business processes and preventing costly rework.

sections.extract: As the steps outlined in Chapter 1 to understand users and the needs for a system to digitize primary health care have shown, creating a PCPOSS is a highly iterative process. Once a team, including technology partners, is in place and an initial set of requirements has been identified, these requirements should be validated with all the key stakeholders. Additional workshops with key stakeholders are necessary to

sections.title: Develop and test prototype design

summary.text: Describes progressive UI design and prototyping across increasing fidelity levels—paper sketches, wireframes, visual mock-ups, and clickable high-fidelity prototypes (Fig. 15)—and details a five-step user-centred design testing cycle (designing test use cases, creating multiple prototypes, validating with end-users via role play, documenting structured feedback, and iterating while guarding against scope creep).

sections.extract: Creating mock-ups of a user interface (UI) and prototyping of the product helps to evaluate the layout, flow and usability of the intended digital application prior to coding and development. These design mock-ups and prototypes will prove useful when the engineers start to build the system, as they will help the engineers to visualize how the functional requirements being built into the system will be used. There

sections.title: Design system architecture

summary.text: Explains how to design a PCPOSS system architecture within a broader Enterprise Architecture (EA) using frameworks such as TOGAF (business, data, application, and technology domains, Table 2) and OpenHIE; defines syntactic, semantic, organizational, and legal interoperability (Table 3); and catalogues global open standards across terminology/classification (WHO-FIC, ICD-11, ICF, ICHI, LOINC, SNOMED-GPS), health content (DAKs, WHO guidelines), communication (HL7 FHIR, IHE, DICOM, GS1), and privacy protection laws (Table 4).

sections.extract: A system architecture is a conceptual model that depicts how the PCPOSS will be structured and how it functions and includes all the software and hardware components that comprise the system. Further, the system architecture of a PCPOSS would need to function within an Enterprise Architecture (EA), which describes how the PCPOSS interacts with other parts of the digital health ecosystem and is used to drive

sections.title: Build and quality assurance

summary.text: Outlines key elements of an agile software build (continuous user engagement, vendor communication, comprehensive documentation, and safety-first quality assurance), specifies seven categories of QA system testing (installation, stress, security, graphic UI, integration, general QA, and accessibility testing), provides the Chapter 4 completion checkpoint, and introduces Chapter 5 (Conduct training, testing and roll-out) with its stakeholder roles, inputs, tools, and outputs.

sections.extract: During this step, the technology partner will take the time to build the PCPOSS. They will need to spend time coding and ensuring that their code results in the required functionality and design. It is easy to underestimate the time and costs needed to build a quality PCPOSS, but it is important to anticipate them properly so that the system is built successfully and meets users’ needs. sections.title: Develop and conduct training

summary.text: Identifies the three categories of training required before wide deployment—training end-users on PCPOSS use, training technical staff on PCPOSS maintenance, and training on clinical service delivery changes (managed by national health programmes)—and recommends piloting the training curriculum on a small scale first.

sections.extract: Three categories of training will be needed: (i) training on use of the PCPOSS; (ii) training on maintenance of the PCPOSS; and (iii) training related to any potential changes to service delivery and quality of care. This Handbook will only address the first two types of training as the third type of training should be addressed by the national health programme managers. The training curriculum should be tested at a

sections.title: Test user acceptance and deployment readiness

summary.text: Describes conducting user acceptance testing (UAT) of the beta PCPOSS with a small group of trained end-users and advisers in real workflows to catch bugs and usability barriers before production roll-out, alongside detailed guidance on culturally tailored, competency-based end-user training (including device familiarization and training of trainers) and ongoing maintenance training for local technology partners.

sections.extract: With a beta version of the PCPOSS available, a series of user acceptance tests needs to take place prior to deployment. User acceptance testing (UAT) should be conducted by the core project team with a small group of trusted advisers and end-users. The small number of UAT testers, including some end-users, should initially be trained on how to use the beta version of the software, then tasked with using the PCPOSS

sections.title: Deploy the system

summary.text: Details the creation of realistic UAT test cases and test data (including edge cases and clinical decision-support verification) and outlines the operational steps led by the technology partner to deploy the validated PCPOSS into a production environment—covering site infrastructure, hardware logistics, software installation, data migration, account configuration, site testing, non-disruptive scheduling, and building user trust.

sections.extract: Deployment of the system often requires strong strategic thinking by the technology partner, as poorly deployed systems can make or break an entire project. 5.2.1 Test cases and test data One way to facilitate UAT is the creation of test cases and associated test data based on use cases that simulate real-time use. Test cases outline how the system should be used and the expected outcomes to test key functionality.

sections.title: Manage feedback and system maintenance

summary.text: Covers establishing standard operating procedures for continuous feedback management, bug resolution, hardware/software maintenance, and post-deployment monitoring and evaluation during roll-out, then introduces Chapter 6 (Prepare for scale-up) with an overview of stakeholder roles, inputs, M&E and MAPS toolkit resources, and outputs for phasing out paper and legacy systems.

sections.extract: Feedback management, training, software updates and hardware maintenance will all be needed continually during the roll-out. The implementation team should have a standard operating procedure for managing all this feedback. For example, if there is a bug that occurs during the pilot and roll-out: • How will the team receive feedback? • Is there a call centre or other central feedback mechanism (e.g. email, secure

sections.title: Determine readiness for scaling up

summary.text: States the prerequisite for scale-up: verifying both that the PCPOSS is technically and operationally ready to scale and that the broader health system is ready to phase out paper and legacy systems.

sections.extract: Before scaling up and phasing out paper and legacy systems, it is important to determine both that the PCPOSS is ready to be scaled up and that the existing health system is ready to phase out paper and legacy systems.

sections.title: Plan for phase-out of legacy system(s)

summary.text: Explains how to assess scale-up readiness using the WHO MAPS toolkit and Digital Health Atlas and how to set SMART (specific, measurable, attainable, relevant, time-bound) objectives and legal/operational policies (including paper backup SOPs for downtime) for phasing out legacy systems, illustrated by Table 5's comprehensive indicators across system functionality, connectivity, power, user adoption, efficiency, care quality, costs, and health outcomes.

sections.extract: When moving from scale-up to integration and sustainability (see Monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions [99]), answer the following question: What targets, indicators or objectives must the PCPOSS meet for the public health authority to feel comfortable phasing out paper and/or legacy systems? Clear, agreed upon objectives should be set to allow for the phase-out of legacy systems. When these

sections.title: Monitor and evaluate progress on objectives

summary.text: Emphasizes establishing a rigorous monitoring and evaluation plan to track progress against scale-up objectives and points implementers, researchers, and policy-makers to WHO's Monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions guide for assessing implementation fidelity and impact.

sections.extract: With clear objectives and indicators to measure progress towards them, it is crucial that the PCPOSS has a clear and robust monitoring and evaluation plan and methodology. WHO offers a practical guide, Monitoring and evaluating digital health interventions (99), with detailed stepwise guidance that is beyond the scope of this handbook. The guidance helps with improving the quality and value of monitoring and

sections.title: Phase-out of legacy system(s)

summary.text: Advises phasing out paper and legacy digital systems in a staged, region-by-region or province-by-province manner rather than waiting for nationwide readiness, enabling manageable resource allocation and cross-provincial learning in coordination with key stakeholders.

sections.extract: Strategically, it is advised to not wait until the entire country is ready to phase out paper systems and/or legacy systems and instead phase out those systems in a staged, or step-wise, manner. For example, if one region or province is ready to phase out paper systems completely, but other provinces are still in the process of adopting PCPOSSs, it might be better to begin the phase out of the paper system in the

sections.title: Adopt change management practices

summary.text: Discusses embedding multi-level change management strategies and cultivating a culture of electronic data use across health workers, supervisors, and programme managers—linking mature data use to SMART Guidelines Layer 5 (Dynamic guidelines and advanced analytics)—while warning that a backup paper system must always remain available for crisis or cybersecurity resilience.

sections.extract: As the PCPOSS is adopted and increasingly integrated into routine use, the phasing out of paper systems entirely will require behaviour change, not just at the level of health workers, but within the public health authority itself. summary.text: Presents Annex 5, a three-column worksheet template ('As a…', 'I want to…', 'So that…') with an obstetric referral example for capturing end-user needs and translating them into functional and non-functional system requirements.

summary.text: Presents Annex 6, a guide defining the six columns of a business process matrix—business process number, process name, process ID (e.g., DAK convention FP.B), participating personas (corresponding to BPMN swim lanes), process objectives, and task set with start/end triggers.

sections.extract: The business process matrix provides an overview of all the key processes that are involved. sections.title: Aggregate indicator mapping guide

summary.text: Presents Annex 9 (a guide for documenting aggregate indicators calculated from point-of-care data, including indicator ID, name, definition, numerator/denominator descriptions and data-dictionary-linked formulas, reporting frequency, disaggregation, targets/alerts, and guideline references), Annex 10 (guides for the decision-support logic overview matrix and scheduling logic overview matrix, with links to five WHO DAKs), and the opening field definitions and DMN hit policy indicators (Unique, Rule order, First) of Annex 11.

sections.extract: A spreadsheet should be created to document the indicators that can be calculated from the individual level data that is collected from the PCPOSS. This guide provides a way to consolidate and organize this list of indicators. What to note Description Indicator ID The Indicator ID should be a running number or letter that would facilitate organization and references. Indicator name Brief name of the indicator.

sections.title: Template for a decision-support table

summary.text: Presents the DMN-adapted decision-support table template for Annex 11—showing how hit policy (U/R/F), rule IDs, conjunctive (same-row AND) and disjunctive (different-row OR) input expressions, system actions, data-element outputs, health worker guidance displays, annotations, and guideline references are structured—along with links to five WHO DAKs containing detailed decision-support table examples.

sections.title: Scheduling logic table guide

summary.text: Presents Annex 12, an illustrative guide and worked example (using the hepatitis B birth dose vaccination schedule) for documenting health service scheduling logic across service name, description, trigger event and date, creation condition, due/overdue/expiration date formulas, completion action, safety risks and alternative schedules, implementation comments, and WHO guideline references.

sections.extract: This illustrative guide can be used to inform how to document health service schedules. The example of the hepatitis B birth dose vaccination schedule is shown here, which is needed to inform clinical decision support. Additional rows for subsequent hepatitis B vaccine doses would be added to complete the hepatitis B vaccination scheduling logic table. sections.title: Prioritization of requirements guide

summary.text: Presents Annex 13, a table guide for transparently documenting and prioritizing system requirements by recording requirement ID, description, type (functional vs. non-functional), priority tier (high/'need-to-have', medium/'should-have', low/'nice-to-have'), stakeholder/guideline/regulatory sources, and stakeholder validation comments.

sections.extract: With a long list of functional and non-functional requirements, but a constrained set of resources (budget and time), it will be critical to ensure an accurate assessment of which functions or features are “need-to-have” (high priority) versus “nice-to-have” (low priority). sections.title: HL7 FHIR standard components

summary.text: Presents Annex 14, defining the core components of the HL7 FHIR standard—FHIR Resources, FHIR Implementation Guides (including their role as SMART Guidelines Layer 3 machine-readable artefacts building on Layer 2 DAKs), FHIR Profiles, FHIR Stores, and FHIR APIs—followed by Annex 14 references and back-matter WHO contact details.

sections.extract: Resources A “FHIR Resource” is a modular component that serves as the basic data exchange format in the HL7 FHIR standard. A FHIR Resource contains the data elements, constraints on those data elements and the data relationships that together make up an exchangeable data model, in the context of health data (1).
